Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Understanding the precise intracellular signalling pathways underpinning hypoxic sensitivity in the carotid body chemoreceptor has been a major unsolved area in sensory neurophysiology. Early studies almost 60 years ago suggested the importance of a metabolic signal coupled to the mitchrondria, which could regulate intracellular calcium homeostasis and exocystosis of excitatory transmitter in type I glomus cells.

Using RNAseq this manuscript has identified a novel gene that encodes protein regulation of Complex IV in the carotid body response to hypoxia. Here the authors found HIGD1C, a novel hypoxia-inducible gene domain factor isoform, as an electron transport chain Complex IV-interacting protein was almost exclusively expressed in the carotid body. Using a combination molecular biology, protein chemistry, genetic knock-out, calcium imaging and respiratory measurements, the authors elegantly demonstrated the physiological utlility of HIGD1C being required for carotid body oxygen sensing via enhanced Complex IV sensitivity to hypoxia. Deletion of the gene massively attenuated the chemoreceptor response to hypoxia, whereas of expression of HIGD1C could recapitulate the increased oxygen sensitivity of Complex IV in HEK 293T cells, but not the response to hypercapnia.

Whilst this large body of work shows the putative role of HIGD1C in oxygen sensing, the relationship between this protein and the graded response of afferent nerve firing to physiological levels of hypoxia remains to be established to support an essential role for this signalling pathway in hypoxic chemotransduction.

This is a large body of work supporting the idea that HIGD1C is required for hypoxic sensing in the mouse through the regulation complex IV. The experiments are well designed, complex and appear to have been carefully performed.

Specific comments for improvement:

Parts of the manuscript are difficult to follow re data presentation since the data are densely reported in places. Eg Figure 1 Figure supplement 2 on page 9 is virtually impossible to read.

A tighter introduction is required re references where credit should be given to the early studies showing that hypoxia excites CB and breathing and chemodenervation abolishes the breathing responses (eg Neil; Torrance; Lahiri should be given credit in para 1 on page 3).

Additionally, primary references should be given for statements of fact like …'Under these pathological conditions, suppressing CB activity improves causal symptoms such as hypertension (REF), cardiac arrhythmias (REF), and insulin resistance (REF) (Iturriaga, 2018)'. Credit must be given to the primary source, not a review.

p 4 'We found that three such genes, Higd1c, Cox4i2, and Ndufa4l2, were expressed at higher levels in the mouse CB (Figure 1A)'. Are you confident that this expression is only in type 1 cells and not type 2 cells?

Much of the data presented has used parametric statistics on n of 3/3 or 4/4 samples eg Figure 1 supp 3 page 10. Are these data normally distributed to support parametric use of stats? Please comment on the sample re biological replicates v technical replicates. How were the data treated here?

The gel on p26 panel B looks over run. Comment?

Aspects of the data are very convincing. Whilst this large body of work shows the putative role of HIGD1C in oxygen sensing, the relationship between this protein and the graded response of afferent nerve firing to physiological levels of hypoxia remains to be established to support an essential role for this signalling pathway in hypoxic chemotransduction. This limitation should be acknowledged. Please comment?

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

I have a number of major concerns about parts of this research which need to be addressed before I could comment on its conclusions and importance. Some of these may just require a better explanation or correction to the text (e.g. where there may be an ambiguity over how an experiment was conducted). Others may require further work

Major comments/Questions

General reporting of results

A very general comment I have about this paper is that numerous experiments, particularly in the latter half of this paper using HEK cells, have been conducted with an 'n' of only 3. I do not know what eLifes's normal expectations/requirements are but I would have thought that an 'n' of at least 4 or 5 independent observations should normally be required. Similarly, numerous gels/blots are presented without any indication of how often these types of experiments were repeated. This should be reported and the journal should have some policy over what is expected. To my mind there could be a substantial amount of further work that needs to be completed before this study could be formally published. Apart from this issue the statistics seem to have been done with suitable care and rigour.

Questions/suggested changes.

Plethysmography.

With respect to the effects of Higd1c KO on ventilation. Although all KO's appear to have a blunted ventilatory response to hypoxia, a ventilatory response remains none the less. This is particularly evident for the 1.1 KO as shown in the example trace in Figure 2 supplement 1 A where the second response to a hypoxic stimulus looks very similar between the KO and normal mouse. This is a somewhat disappointing result in that it may limit the conclusions that can be drawn from this study. One could have hoped that a Higd1c KO would either eliminate the response to hypoxia or had no effect at all. As this is a very important piece of evidence I want to ask for more detail regarding the data and methods.

Forgive me if I have misunderstood but in the methods section you state that "we used a respiratory rate of 215 breaths/min (comparable to the mean of a wild type in hypoxia) as a cut off for inclusion in this study". It is unclear how this works. Are you rejecting recordings with RR in excess of this figure or below this figure? When are you making this decision, under normoxic conditions at the beginning of an experiment, under hypoxic conditions, or at any time in the recording? Can you clarify this point and indicate how often recordings were rejected by this criteria in the different mice?

Was there any notable difference in mouse behaviour between genotypes during plethysmography? Mice usually become much less active in hypoxia and basal metabolic rate goes down resulting in a fall in CO2 production and a drop in PaCO2 which leads to a fall in ventilation (hypoxic ventilatory decline: HVD). This often complicates the analysis/interpretation of responses to hypoxia. Over what time period do you measure changes in ventilation – over the entire period of exposure to hypoxia, at the peak? Or towards the end? Are changes in the rate of HVD influencing the comparison between KO and wt? Have you measured PaCO2 under hypoxic conditions? I would predict that it would be lower than under control conditions. Could you introduce a little CO2 in hypoxic conditions to try to neutralise this effect?

What happens if you do a sham switch (i.e. switch between two identical gasses/air), is there any startle response associated with just mechanically switching between two gas lines? If not what happens if you look specifically at the peak/early response to hypoxia before CO2 has much chance to fall?

Are Higd1c +/+ mice taken from your in house breeding programs generating Higd1c -/- mice or are they just off the shelf C57Bl/6J from Jax? If the latter how long are these mice held in your facility (under the same conditions as the KO mice) before being used?

Nerve fibre recordings and calcium recordings.

In the methods section on nerve recordings you state that "Preparations were exposed to a brief hypoxic challenge (PO2 = 60 mmHg) to determine viability; preparations that failed to show a clear increase in activity during this challenge were discarded". You are testing the hypothesis that Higd1c is important/essential for the generation of the response to hypoxia so why exclude data from preparations that lack a hypoxic response? This is just what you are looking for! I hope this is just a mistake in writing up the methods, BUT if this is really what was done then the whole nerve recording study could be invalid (depending on just what proportion of preparations were actually discarded). If you want some sort of test for viability of the preparation, which is a good idea, then there are many other stimuli one could choose instead that do not involve mitochondrial function e.g hypercapnia/acidosis, high potassium, acetyl choline, TASK channel inhibitors/respiratory stimulants.

One of the key issues regarding the role of alternative mitochondrial subunits in the carotid body is not simply that they may affect the maximal turnover rate of cytochrome oxidase but whether they alter the kinetic parameters defining sensitivity to hypoxia (i.e. Km, oxygen affinity, P50 ). To determine these really requires making a number of measurements at different PO2 including a zero point (anoxia). This could have been done for both nerve recordings and calcium measurements. Unfortunately it was not, so we are left with data from both of these experiments which demonstrates that the response to hypoxia is smaller in the KO but we have no idea whether these kinetic parameters have changed or not. The study would be a lot stronger if you could demonstrate a change in Km in the Higd1c KO.

Rh123 experiments.

It would appear from the results obtained with Rh123 and the weak responses to FCCP that there was inadequate loading of this dye to make good measurements of mitochondrial potential (ψM) in many of the cells studied. If you look at the paper by Biscoe and Duchen they were achieving a 100% increase in Rh125 fluorescence upon adding FCCP, Anoxia or CN, not 20%. The level of loading is critical with this dye in order to get it to work properly in the de-quench mode. In addition, to correct for differences in dye loading, responses to acute hypoxia should probably be normalised not only to the baseline but also to the response to FCCP. The smaller response to hypoxia in Higd1c -/- could simply reflect lower dye loading, with consequent lower dynamic response from Rh123 to change in mitochondrial potential, rather than any actual change in ψM.

The response to anoxia has not been tested which again confounds attempts to determine a P50 for mitochondrial depolarisation. I note that the rate of change in PO2 (Figure 4 suppl 1 A) is rather slow so some Rh123 may also leak out of the cell during the recording. Were any corrections applied for dye leakage?

In summary the interpretation of this data is equivocal. Higd1c -/- may take up Rh123 less avidly than wt but is this due to a lower resting ψM or something else? This experiment needs repeating extending loading time or Rh123 concentration until robust responses to FCCP can be recorded.

If you want to see if genotype affects resting ψM you would probably be better not working in the quench mode but either using much lower concentrations of Rh123 or another probe, e.g. TMRM, and loading for a longer period of time (until dye uptake reaches a steady state without any quenching occuring).

CIV sensitivity to Hypoxia in HEK.

Data in Fig6-E shows >= 40% inhibition of oxygen consumption under hypoxic conditions compared to normoxia in all HEK cell types studied. Given that the level of oxygen in hypoxia is stated to be 25 mmHg this is something of a surprise. The P50 for most cells is thought to be < 1mmHg. Something is wrong here. If you are using an Oroboros Oxygraph (as stated in methods) it should be possible to measure oxygen consumption from air all the way down to zero oxygen and derive an exact P50 for each cell type. This should be done. This is a very important experiment that proports to show that it is the combination of Higd1c and Cox4I2 that generates the unusual sensitivity of complex IV towards oxygen. Philosophically I like this hypothesis. If true it would mark a major advance in this field, but I want to see some hard data with rigorously determined kinetic measurements!

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

This paper uses a range of techniques to demonstrate the presence of a novel protein (HIGD1C) that interacts with complex 4 of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. The authors demonstrate that this protein is required for hypoxic chemotransduction at the level of the whole animal (plethysmography), at the level of the in-vitro organ (carotid sinus nerve recordings) and at the level of the glomus cell (calcium imaging). The authors then go on to demonstrate that HIGD1C may interact and alter the sensitivity of complex 4 to hypoxia.

The authors are to be congratulated on a set of thorough physiological experiments that are then extended by detailed cellular respiration studies. Working with mouse carotid body tissue is incredibly challenging and the authors have done extremely well to get such high quality and valuable data.

The combination of genetic, physiological and cellular experiments make this an extremely compelling paper suitable for publication in eLife.

The question of why carotid body glomus cells are unusually sensitive to hypoxia has troubled researchers for decades. This paper makes an extremely compelling case for the expression of HIGD1C modulating complex 4 and thereby sensitizing it to hypoxia. The data seems strong and the paper is likely to have a major impact in the field of oxygen sensing.

There are several observations that would greatly strengthen the paper.

1. It would be better in future if the calcium imaging studies could be performed using the same perfused preparation that the nerve recording experiments used. This would remove the requirement for equilibrating superfusate with 95% oxygen which is far from physiological and would allow the carotid body tissue to be perfused with physiologically relevant levels of oxygen. However, superfusion with hyperoxic solutions is considered standard in many systems and so additional experiments are not required at this time.

2. Expanding the study to see if HIGD1C is expressed in carotid bodies of multiple species would strengthen the paper. It would also be interesting to see if it is absent in the carotid bodies of guinea pigs which are not acutely oxygen sensitive. Furthermore, chromaffin cells in fetal adrenal medulla are oxygen-sensitive whereas mature chromaffin cells are not, it would be fascinating to see if HIGD1C expression changes during the maturation of chromaffin cells. These possibilities might be discussed.

3. Tidal volume changes with the weight of the animals. Tidal volume should be adjusted for the weights of the animals tested. If there are weight differences between knockouts and wildtype it can have profound effects on the data.

claims.claim: Higd1c is expressed in mouse kidney proximal tubules.

claims.claim: Higd1c is enriched in a population of cells in the CB essential for oxygen sensing.

claims.claim: Heterozygous Higd1c mutant mice were fertile.

claims.claim: Homozygous Higd1c mutants were viable and not underrepresented in the progeny.
claims.source: For all three alleles, heterozygous Higd1c mutant mice were fertile, and homozygous mutants were viable and not underrepresented in the progeny (Table 1).

claims.claim: In 1-1 and 5-3 alleles, Higd1c mRNA levels were reduced by 40–90% in CBs and kidneys from Higd1c-/- mutants compared to Higd1c+/+ animals.

claims.claim: Higd1c-/- mutants of all three alleles had normal ventilation in normoxia.

claims.claim: Higd1c-/- mutants of all three alleles were defective in the hypoxic ventilatory response.

claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-body plethysmography data shown in Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–M.

claims.claim: The defects observed in Higd1c alleles were at least as severe as ablation or denervation of the CBs in rodents.

claims.claim: Higd1c-/- mice maintained robust ventilatory responses to hypercapnia comparable to Higd1c+/+ animals.

claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-body plethysmography data shown in Figure 2E–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–J.

claims.claim: Higd1c specifically regulates ventilatory responses to hypoxia.
claims.source: These results suggest that Higd1c specifically regulates ventilatory responses to hypoxia.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the selective defect in hypoxic but not hypercapnic ventilatory responses.

claims.claim: Baseline CSN activity was similar between Higd1c 1-1+/+ and Higd1c 1-1-/- tissues.

claims.claim: CSN activity increased in a dose-dependent manner in response to decreasing oxygen levels in Higd1c 1-1+/+ tissue.

claims.evidence: This is supported by carotid sinus nerve recording data shown in Figure 3A and D.

claims.claim: The response to hypoxia was attenuated in CSNs from Higd1c 1-1-/- mutants.

claims.claim: The response to high CO2/H+ was unaffected in CSNs from Higd1c 1-1-/- mutants.
claims.source: However, while this response to hypoxia was attenuated in CSNs from Higd1c 1-1-/- mutants (Figure 3B and D), the response to high CO2/H+ was unaffected (Figure 3A–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by carotid sinus nerve recording data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claims.claim: HIGD1C specifically mediates oxygen sensing at the level of the whole CB organ.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that HIGD1C specifically mediates oxygen sensing at the level of the whole CB organ.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the selective defect in hypoxic but not hypercapnic responses in CSN recordings.

claims.claim: Glomus cells from Higd1c 1-1-/- mutants mounted a weaker calcium response to hypoxia than those from Higd1c 1-1+/+ animals.
claims.source: We found that glomus cells from Higd1c 1-1-/- mutants mounted a weaker calcium response to hypoxia than those from Higd1c 1-1+/+ animals, with fewer glomus cells responding strongly to both levels of hypoxia (Figure 3E–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E.

claims.claim: Glomus cells from Higd1c 1-1-/- mutants were not significantly different from Higd1c 1-1+/+ animals in their calcium response to low pH or high KCl.
claims.source: In contrast to hypoxia, glomus cells from Higd1c 1-1-/- mutants were not significantly different from Higd1c 1-1+/+ animals in their calcium response to low pH or high KCl compared to glomus cells from Higd1c 1-1-/- animals (Figure 3E–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E–H.

claims.claim: Calcium responses to cyanide were similar between Higd1c 1-1+/+ and Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells.
claims.source: Calcium responses to cyanide, a potent ETC CIV inhibitor, were also similar between Higd1c 1-1+/+ and Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells (Figure 3E–H), suggesting that strong ETC inhibition is still able to trigger sensory responses in glomus cells mutated in Higd1c like other mutants with defects in CB oxygen sensing (Peng et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E–H and citations to other studies.

claims.claim: HIGD1C contributes specifically to glomus cell responses to hypoxia.
claims.source: Together, these results show that HIGD1C contributes specifically to glomus cell responses to hypoxia.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the selective defect in hypoxic responses in calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells had an attenuated response to hypoxia measured by rhodamine 123 fluorescence.
claims.source: Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells had an attenuated response to hypoxia and a higher percentage of cells that responded poorly to FCCP, a potent uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation that depolarizes the IMM (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rhodamine 123 imaging data shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells had a higher percentage of cells that responded poorly to FCCP.
claims.source: Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells had an attenuated response to hypoxia and a higher percentage of cells that responded poorly to FCCP, a potent uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation that depolarizes the IMM (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rhodamine 123 imaging data shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: The IMM is less polarized at baseline in Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells.
claims.source: The weaker response of Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells to FCCP was evident even when FCCP was presented as the first stimulus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the IMM is less polarized at baseline in mutant glomus cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the weaker FCCP response when presented as the first stimulus.

claims.claim: In glomus cells that had a strong FCCP response > 0.2, Rh123 fluorescence was greater in Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells in normoxia (PO2 = 100 mmHg).
claims.source: This idea is also supported by the observation that in glomus cells that had a strong FCCP response > 0.2, Rh123 fluorescence was greater in Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells in normoxia (PO2 = 100 mmHg) (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rhodamine 123 imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The increase in Rh123 fluorescence in hypoxia (PO2 < 80 mmHg) was smaller in Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells than in Higd1c 1-1+/+ glomus cells.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the increase in fluorescence in hypoxia (PO2 < 80 mmHg) was smaller than in Higd1c 1-1+/+ glomus cells (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rhodamine 123 imaging data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: The pattern of weaker ETC activity in normoxia that cannot be suppressed further in hypoxia seen in Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells resembles that of acute CII inhibition on CB sensory activity.
claims.source: This pattern of weaker ETC activity in normoxia that cannot be suppressed further in hypoxia seen in Higd1c 1-1-/- glomus cells resembles that of acute CII inhibition on CB sensory activity (Swiderska et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to a published study on CII inhibition.

claims.claim: Vascular cells in Higd1c 1-1+/+ CBs had a left-shifted IMM potential response to hypoxia compared to glomus cells.
claims.source: In Higd1c 1-1+/+ CBs, we found that vascular cells, which are less oxygen-sensitive than glomus cells, had a left-shifted IMM potential response to hypoxia (Figure 4G–I), indicating that our hypoxic stimulus was in an appropriate range to detect the enhanced oxygen sensitivity of the CB over other cell types.
claims.evidence: This is supported by rhodamine 123 imaging data shown in Figure 4G–I.

claims.claim: HIGD1C enhances ETC inhibition by hypoxia in glomus cells.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that HIGD1C enhances ETC inhibition by hypoxia in glomus cells, a response linked to CB sensory activity (Chang, 2017; Holmes et al., 2018; Ortega-Sáenz and López-Barneo, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the rhodamine 123 imaging data and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Overexpressed FLAG-tagged HIGD1C associated with ETC CIV and cytochrome c in wild-type HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Overexpressed FLAG-tagged HIGD1C associated with ETC CIV and cytochrome c (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: HIGD1C overexpression severely reduced the abundance of ETC supercomplexes in wild-type HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Notably, HIGD1C overexpression severely reduced the abundance of ETC supercomplexes, and supercomplexes that did assemble contained only traces of in-gel CIV activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BN-PAGE and in-gel activity data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claims.claim: Defects in supercomplex formation caused by HIGD1C overexpression correlated with a decrease in CIV enzymatic activity in wild-type HEK293T cells.
claims.source: These defects in supercomplex formation correlated with a decrease in CIV enzymatic activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity and oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-I.

claims.claim: HIGD1C associated with CIV and cytochrome c in HIGD1A-KO and HIGD2A-KO mutant cells.
claims.source: As in wild-type cells, HIGD1C associated with CIV and cytochrome c in HIGD1A-KO and HIGD2A-KO mutant cells (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–C.

claims.claim: HIGD1C did not associate with CIII in HIGD1A-KO and HIGD2A-KO mutant cells.
claims.source: Unlike HIGD1A, HIGD1C did not associate with CIII and could not rescue defects in the assembly of supercomplexes in either HIGD1A-KO or HIGD2A-KO cells (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D; Timón-Gómez et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: HIGD1C could not rescue defects in the assembly of supercomplexes in HIGD1A-KO or HIGD2A-KO cells.
claims.source: Unlike HIGD1A, HIGD1C did not associate with CIII and could not rescue defects in the assembly of supercomplexes in either HIGD1A-KO or HIGD2A-KO cells (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D; Timón-Gómez et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: HIGD1C overexpression restored CIV activity in HIGD1A-KO cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, however, HIGD1C overexpression restored CIV activity in HIGD1A-KO, but not HIGD2A-KO cells (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity data shown in Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3E and F.

claims.claim: HIGD1C overexpression did not restore CIV activity in HIGD2A-KO cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, however, HIGD1C overexpression restored CIV activity in HIGD1A-KO, but not HIGD2A-KO cells (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity data shown in Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3E and F.

claims.claim: Cellular respiration at the overall ETC level was restored by HIGD1C overexpression in HIGD1A-KO cells.
claims.source: Supporting this idea, we observed that cellular respiration at the overall ETC level was also restored by HIGD1C overexpression in HIGD1A-KO cells (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: Overexpression of mouse HIGD1C induced a weaker rescue of CIV activity than human HIGD1C in HIGD1A-KO cells.
claims.source: Overexpression of mouse HIGD1C induced a weaker rescue of CIV activity than human HIGD1C, likely due to disruption of species-specific associations between ETC subunits (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: Mouse HIGD1C fully rescued mitochondrial oxygen consumption in HIGD1A-KO cells due to the spare respiratory capacity of the ETC.
claims.source: Nonetheless, mouse HIGD1C fully rescued mitochondrial oxygen consumption due to the spare respiratory capacity of the ETC (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: HIGD1C is not involved in ETC complex or supercomplex biogenesis.
claims.source: These rescue experiments show that HIGD1C is not involved in ETC complex or supercomplex biogenesis, but similarly to HIGD1A, it can interact with CIV to regulate its activity.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the inability of HIGD1C to rescue supercomplex assembly defects.

claims.claim: HIGD1C can interact with CIV to regulate its activity similarly to HIGD1A.
claims.source: These rescue experiments show that HIGD1C is not involved in ETC complex or supercomplex biogenesis, but similarly to HIGD1A, it can interact with CIV to regulate its activity.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the ability of HIGD1C to restore CIV activity in HIGD1A-KO cells.

claims.claim: The absence of HIGD1A produced a blue shift in the peak of heme a+a3 absorbance from 603 nm to 599 nm.
claims.source: The absence of HIGD1A produced a blue shift in the peak of heme a+a3 absorbance from 603 nm to 599 nm (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) that is associated with changes around the CIV heme a centers (Shapleigh et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The spectral shift in HIGD1A-KO cells was completely restored by expressing HIGD1A.
claims.source: Previous studies showed that adding excess recombinant HIGD1A to highly purified oxidized CIV increases CIV activity twofold and changes the conformation around the heme a center (Hayashi et al., 2015), suggesting that HIGD1A levels modulate CIV activity. Here, the spectral shift observed in the HIGD1A-KO cell line was completely restored by expressing HIGD1A (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Expression of human or mouse HIGD1C generated a broader peak in the heme a+a3 absorbance spectrum.
claims.source: While the wavelength at the peak appeared to be restored by human HIGD1C, expression of human or mouse HIGD1C generated a broader peak, probably due to the existence of a mixed population of the enzyme, to partially restore the spectral shift (Figure 6A–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 6A–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: A blue shift in the wavelength at the peak was apparent in HIGD1A-KO cells overexpressing mouse HIGD1C alone or human HIGD1C and COX4I2 together.
claims.source: A blue shift in the wavelength at the peak was apparent in HIGD1A-KO cells overexpressing the mouse HIGD1C alone or human HIGD1C and COX4I2 together (Figure 6A–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that the atypical CIV subunit COX4I2 expressed in the CB (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and C) can modify the effect of HIGD1C overexpression.
claims.evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 6A–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: The spectral shift caused by HIGD1C and COX4I2 resembled the unusual absorbance spectrum of cytochromes found in the CB.
claims.source: In addition, this spectral shift resembled the unusual absorbance spectrum of cytochromes found in the CB (Streller et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to a published study on CB cytochrome spectra.

claims.claim: Interaction of HIGD1C with CIV can alter the active site and activity of CIV.
claims.source: These results suggest that interaction of HIGD1C with CIV can alter the active site and activity of CIV.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the spectral changes and activity measurements.

claims.claim: Co-expression of HIGD1C and COX4I2 in HIGD1A-KO cells decreased CIV-dependent respiration in hypoxia more than wild-type and other cell lines.
claims.source: Co-expression of HIGD1C and COX4I2 in HIGD1A-KO cells, which better models the ETC composition in the CB (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and C), decreased CIV-dependent respiration in hypoxia more than wild-type and other cell lines, including one overexpressing HIGD1C alone (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Co-expression of HIGD1C and COX4I2 increased the oxygen pressure at half-maximal respiration (p50mito), suggesting a reduction in oxygen affinity.
claims.source: This condition also increased the oxygen pressure at half-maximal respiration (p50mito), suggesting a reduction in oxygen affinity (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by oxygen kinetics data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Overexpression of COX4I2 alone decreased p50mito in HIGD1A-KO cells.
claims.source: In HIGD1A-KO cells, overexpression of COX4I2 alone decreased p50mito, but additional expression of HIGD1C further modified the JO2/Jmax curve to increase p50mito over wild-type (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by oxygen kinetics data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Additional expression of HIGD1C with COX4I2 further modified the JO2/Jmax curve to increase p50mito over wild-type in HIGD1A-KO cells.
claims.source: In HIGD1A-KO cells, overexpression of COX4I2 alone decreased p50mito, but additional expression of HIGD1C further modified the JO2/Jmax curve to increase p50mito over wild-type (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by oxygen kinetics data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Co-overexpression of HIGD1C and COX4I2 can confer hypersensitivity to hypoxia in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that co-overexpression of HIGD1C and COX4I2, two atypical mitochondrial ETC proteins expressed in CB glomus cells that mediate oxygen sensing (Moreno-Domínguez et al., 2020), can confer hypersensitivity to hypoxia in HEK293T cells.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the oxygen consumption and kinetics data in Figure 6E-F.

claims.claim: The COX4I2-containing CIV and its regulation by HIGD1C emerge as necessary and sufficient factors to promote oxygen sensing by CB glomus cells.
claims.source: Therefore, the COX4I2-containing CIV, and its regulation by HIGD1C, emerge as necessary and sufficient factors to promote oxygen sensing by CB glomus cells.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the combined genetic and cell culture data.

claims.claim: HIGD1C interacts with CIV to alter the conformation of its enzymatic active center.
claims.source: Here, we identified HIGD1C as a novel mitochondrial CIV protein expressed almost exclusively in CB glomus cells that is essential for oxygen sensing by the CB (summarized in Figure 7A and B). We found that HIGD1C interacts with CIV to alter the conformation of its enzymatic active center.
claims.evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis data in Figure 6A-D.

claims.claim: Overexpression of COX4I2 increased the stability of HIGD1C in HIGD1A-KO cells.
claims.source: In the absence of HIGD1A, co-overexpression of HIGD1C and COX4I2 increased oxygen sensitivity of CIV in HEK293T cells (Figure 6E), and overexpression of COX4I2 increased the stability of HIGD1C (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: COX4I1 associates with HIGD1A in CIV assembly.
claims.source: Since COX4I1, the ubiquitously expressed COX4 subunit, associates with HIGD1A in CIV assembly (Timón-Gómez et al., 2020b), the alternative COX4I2 subunit may assemble with HIGD1C.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The alternative COX4I2 subunit may assemble with HIGD1C.
claims.source: Since COX4I1, the ubiquitously expressed COX4 subunit, associates with HIGD1A in CIV assembly (Timón-Gómez et al., 2020b), the alternative COX4I2 subunit may assemble with HIGD1C.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the increased stability of HIGD1C with COX4I2 overexpression.

claims.claim: COX4I2 overexpression in the presence of HIGD1A in WT cells decreases HIGD1C abundance.
claims.source: In opposition to its effect in HIGD1A-KO cells, COX4I2 overexpression in the presence of HIGD1A in WT cells decreases HIGD1C abundance, suggesting that HIGD1A and HIGD1C interact with CIV in the same domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: HIGD1A and HIGD1C interact with CIV in the same domains.
claims.source: In opposition to its effect in HIGD1A-KO cells, COX4I2 overexpression in the presence of HIGD1A in WT cells decreases HIGD1C abundance, suggesting that HIGD1A and HIGD1C interact with CIV in the same domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the competitive effects of HIGD1A and HIGD1C.

claims.claim: Coalitions of different CIV proteins may assemble under varying conditions and perform distinct physiological functions.
claims.source: These results indicate that coalitions of different CIV proteins may assemble under varying conditions and perform distinct physiological functions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the different effects of HIGD1C and COX4I2 in different cellular contexts.

claims.claim: HIGD1C is evolutionarily closer to HIGD1A than to HIGD2A.
claims.source: HIGD1C is evolutionarily closer to HIGD1A than to HIGD2A (Timón-Gómez et al., 2020a), which could explain why in normoxic conditions HIGD1C is able to substitute for HIGD1A function partially but not for HIGD2A (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation and functional data.

claims.claim: HIGD1C does not perform any apparent role in assembling the ETC complexes or supercomplexes.
claims.source: Unlike HIGD1A and HIGD2A, HIGD1C does not perform any apparent role in assembling the ETC complexes or supercomplexes (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: HIGD1C promotes CIV enzymatic activity in normoxia like HIGD1A.
claims.source: HIGD1C interacts with cytochrome c and CIV (Figure 5A and B) and, like HIGD1A, promotes CIV enzymatic activity in normoxia (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: HIGD1C serves as a negative modulator of CIV activity or is less efficient than HIGD1A in promoting CIV activity under limiting oxygen conditions.
claims.source: However, whereas HIGD1A is a positive regulator of CIV (Hayashi et al., 2015), our data indicate that HIGD1C serves as a negative modulator of CIV activity or is less efficient than HIGD1A in promoting CIV activity under limiting oxygen conditions (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the oxygen consumption data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: HIGD1C does not act in a CIV formed by standard subunits but in a CIV containing atypical tissue-specific isoforms such as COX4I2.
claims.source: Importantly, HIGD1C does not act in a CIV formed by standard subunits but in a CIV containing atypical tissue-specific isoforms known to be regulated by hypoxia, such as COX4I2, because increased sensitivity of the ETC to hypoxia is apparent only when both HIGD1C and COX4I2 are overexpressed (Figure 6E and F).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the oxygen consumption and kinetics data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claims.claim: The interaction of HIGD1C with hypoxic CIV containing atypical subunits results in an oxygen-sensing cytochrome c oxidase enzyme in CB glomus cells.
claims.source: Our data allow us to conclude that the interaction of HIGD1C with hypoxic CIV containing atypical subunits results in an oxygen-sensing cytochrome c oxidase enzyme in CB glomus cells.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the combined data on HIGD1C and COX4I2 effects.

claims.claim: Additional components are likely required to fully reconstitute the oxygen sensitivity of CB glomus cells beyond HIGD1C and COX4I2.
claims.source: However, while we demonstrated here that HIGD1C and COX4I2 are sufficient to confer oxygen sensitivity to CIV in HEK293T cells, additional components are likely to be required to fully reconstitute the oxygen sensitivity of CB glomus cells.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the complexity of CB oxygen sensing.

claims.claim: NDUFA4L2, COX8B, and PCX are attractive candidates for further study to determine their potential contribution to CB oxygen sensing.
claims.source: Other proteins upregulated in glomus cells, such as the atypical CIV subunits NDUFA4L2 and COX8B and the glycolytic enzyme PCX (Chang et al., 2015; Moreno-Domínguez et al., 2020), are attractive candidates for further study to determine their potential contribution to CB oxygen sensing.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on expression data and previous studies.

claims.claim: The expression of three atypical CIV subunits in the CB correlates with the sufficiency of CIV alone to recapitulate the unusual oxygen dose response of the ETC in glomus cells.
claims.source: The expression of three atypical CIV subunits in the CB correlates with the sufficiency of CIV alone to recapitulate the unusual oxygen dose response of the ETC in glomus cells (Buckler and Turner, 2013), suggesting that CIV is key for CB oxygen sensing.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the established physiological role of carotid body (CB) chemoreceptors as oxygen sensors that trigger rapid cardiorespiratory reflexes in response to hypoxia, essential for maintaining tissue oxygenation in vital organs.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C9-C12 describe well-established knowledge about CB function supported by multiple historical and contemporary citations. These claims provide necessary background context and are appropriately supported by the literature.

results.result: Under pathological conditions including sleep-disorder breathing, hypertension, and metabolic syndrome, the CB becomes hyperactive, and suppressing CB activity improves symptoms such as hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, and insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 are supported by multiple citations to published studies demonstrating therapeutic benefits of CB suppression in various disease states. This provides important clinical context for understanding CB function.

results.result: The mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC), particularly complexes I and IV, mediates acute oxygen sensing in CB glomus cells, with prior studies showing that Ndufs2 and Cox4i2 knockouts attenuate CB sensory activity and that glomus cell mitochondria exhibit enhanced oxygen sensitivity compared to other cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C24 are well-supported by citations to historical work (Heymans) and recent genetic studies. These establish the mechanistic framework and prior knowledge upon which the current study builds, providing appropriate context for the novel findings about HIGD1C.

results.result: HIGD1C is a novel hypoxia-inducible gene domain factor that is almost exclusively expressed in CB glomus cells at 30-600,000-fold higher levels than other tissues, with expression confirmed by RNAseq, RT-qPCR, and in situ hybridization in mouse, rat, and human CB.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C5, C29, C31-C33, C36-C37, C39-C42 are strongly supported by multiple complementary expression analyses (RNAseq, RT-qPCR, in situ hybridization) across species. The tissue-specific expression pattern is consistently demonstrated with appropriate controls and quantification (Figure 1 and supplements).

results.result: HIGD1C is targeted to mitochondria and co-localizes with the mitochondrial marker HSP60 when overexpressed in HEK293T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C34-C35 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1C) showing co-localization with HSP60. However, this is based on overexpression in a heterologous system; endogenous localization in CB glomus cells would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: HIGD1C is not generally necessary for mitochondrial function, as evidenced by the viability and normal Mendelian ratios of Higd1c knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C43-C44 are supported by breeding data (Table 1) showing normal viability and inheritance patterns. This inference is reasonable given the tissue-specific expression pattern, though more comprehensive metabolic phenotyping of other tissues would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Higd1c knockout mice (three independent alleles) exhibit normal ventilation in normoxia but severe defects in hypoxic ventilatory responses comparable to CB ablation, while maintaining normal hypercapnic responses, indicating HIGD1C specifically regulates oxygen sensing.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 are strongly supported by whole-body plethysmography data from three independent alleles (Figure 2 and supplements). The specificity for hypoxic vs. hypercapnic responses is well-demonstrated with appropriate statistical analyses and effect sizes (Cohen's d = 1.24-2.13 for hypoxic response). The consistency across alleles strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Carotid sinus nerve (CSN) recordings show that HIGD1C specifically mediates oxygen sensing at the CB organ level, with Higd1c-/- mutants exhibiting attenuated responses to hypoxia but normal responses to hypercapnia.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by ex vivo CSN recordings (Figure 3A-D) showing dose-dependent responses to oxygen levels in wild-type tissue and attenuated responses in mutants. The selectivity for oxygen vs. CO2/H+ responses is clearly demonstrated, though sample sizes are modest (n=7-10 preparations).

results.result: Glomus cells from Higd1c-/- mutants exhibit weaker calcium responses to hypoxia with fewer strongly responding cells, while maintaining normal responses to low pH, high KCl, and cyanide, demonstrating HIGD1C specifically contributes to hypoxic responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 3E-H, supplements) from large numbers of cells (201-312 cells from 3-5 animals). The selective defect in hypoxic responses with preserved responses to other stimuli is well-demonstrated. The cyanide response suggests strong ETC inhibition can bypass HIGD1C requirement.

results.result: HIGD1C enhances ETC inhibition by hypoxia in glomus cells, as demonstrated by rhodamine 123 imaging showing attenuated hypoxic responses, reduced baseline mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhanced oxygen sensitivity compared to vascular cells in Higd1c-/- mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 are supported by rhodamine 123 imaging data (Figure 4 and supplements) showing altered mitochondrial membrane potential responses. The pattern resembles CII inhibition effects (C65), providing mechanistic context. The comparison to vascular cells (C66) validates the experimental oxygen range. However, rhodamine 123 can have complex loading and quenching properties that may complicate interpretation.

results.result: In heterologous HEK293T cells, HIGD1C associates with complex IV and cytochrome c, does not rescue supercomplex assembly defects in HIGD1A-KO or HIGD2A-KO cells, but specifically restores CIV activity and cellular respiration in HIGD1A-KO cells, indicating HIGD1C regulates CIV activity rather than assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C80 are supported by comprehensive biochemical analyses including co-immunoprecipitation, BN-PAGE, enzymatic assays, and respirometry (Figure 5 and supplements). The differential rescue of HIGD1A-KO vs. HIGD2A-KO cells is well-demonstrated. The species-specific effects (C77-C78) are appropriately noted. However, overexpression artifacts in heterologous cells may not fully recapitulate endogenous CB physiology.

results.result: HIGD1C alters the conformation of the CIV active site, as demonstrated by spectral analysis showing that HIGD1C expression produces a broader peak and blue shift in heme a+a3 absorbance, particularly when co-expressed with COX4I2, resembling the unusual cytochrome spectrum found in CB.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 are supported by UV/Vis spectroscopy data (Figure 6A-D, supplements) showing spectral shifts associated with CIV active site changes. The comparison to CB cytochrome spectra (C85) provides physiological relevance. However, the interpretation of 'broader peaks' as 'mixed populations' (C83) is speculative, and the spectral measurements have inherent technical limitations.

results.result: Co-expression of HIGD1C and COX4I2 in HIGD1A-KO cells confers hypersensitivity to hypoxia, decreasing CIV-dependent respiration in hypoxia and increasing p50mito, demonstrating that COX4I2-containing CIV regulated by HIGD1C is necessary and sufficient for CB oxygen sensing.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by high-resolution respirometry data (Figure 6E-F, supplements) showing enhanced oxygen sensitivity when both HIGD1C and COX4I2 are co-expressed. The p50mito measurements provide quantitative evidence for altered oxygen affinity. However, the 'necessary and sufficient' conclusion (C92) is strong given this is a heterologous system; additional components may be required in vivo (acknowledged in C106).

results.result: HIGD1C interacts with CIV to alter its enzymatic active center conformation, with COX4I2 increasing HIGD1C stability in HIGD1A-KO cells, suggesting COX4I2 may assemble with HIGD1C while HIGD1A and HIGD1C compete for the same CIV binding domains, indicating different CIV protein coalitions may assemble under varying conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 integrate multiple lines of evidence including spectral analysis, stability measurements, and competitive effects. The inference about COX4I2-HIGD1C assembly (C96) is reasonable but indirect. The competitive binding model (C97-C98) is supported by immunoblot data but would benefit from direct binding studies. The speculation about 'coalitions' (C99) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: HIGD1C is evolutionarily closer to HIGD1A than HIGD2A, does not assemble ETC complexes or supercomplexes, promotes CIV activity in normoxia like HIGD1A but serves as a negative modulator or is less efficient under hypoxia, and specifically acts in CIV containing atypical subunits like COX4I2 to create an oxygen-sensing enzyme.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C105 synthesize multiple experimental observations into a mechanistic model. The evolutionary relationship (C100) is cited. The lack of assembly function (C101) is demonstrated by BN-PAGE. The differential activity in normoxia vs. hypoxia (C102-C103) is supported by enzymatic and respirometry data. The requirement for atypical subunits (C104-C105) is well-demonstrated by the synergistic effects of HIGD1C and COX4I2.

results.result: While HIGD1C and COX4I2 are sufficient to confer oxygen sensitivity to CIV in HEK293T cells, additional components including NDUFA4L2, COX8B, and PCX are likely required to fully reconstitute CB glomus cell oxygen sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 appropriately acknowledge limitations and suggest future directions. This is a reasonable speculation based on the complexity of CB oxygen sensing and the expression of other atypical proteins. The authors appropriately temper their conclusions about sufficiency.

results.result: The expression of atypical CIV subunits in CB correlates with CIV's sufficiency for oxygen sensing, and HIGD1C may modulate ETC activity in other oxygen-sensitive tissues like kidney proximal tubules, though HIGD1C is not expressed in lung despite COX4I2's role in hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C114 provide broader context and speculation about HIGD1C function. The correlation with CIV sufficiency (C108) is supported by citation. The tissue-specific roles (C109-C113) are appropriately cited. The speculation about kidney function (C114) is reasonable given HIGD1C expression there but remains speculative without functional data.

results.result: Due to imaging resolution limitations, HIGD1C may be expressed in both glomus cells and sustentacular glial-like cells that are proposed to cooperate in CB sensory signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 appropriately acknowledge technical limitations of in situ hybridization. The possibility of expression in sustentacular cells is reasonable given their proposed cooperation with glomus cells (cited), but this remains unresolved and would require higher-resolution techniques or cell-type-specific markers.

results.result: HIGD1C is critical for CB oxygen sensing and metabolic responses to hypoxia in mice, regulates CIV activity and conformation in cell culture, and when co-expressed with COX4I2 enhances CIV oxygen sensitivity, with HIGD1C and COX4I2 proposed as key components conferring extreme oxygen sensitivity to CB glomus cell mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 represent the central conclusions of the manuscript, integrating in vivo mouse phenotypes (C25) with cell culture mechanistic studies (C26-C27). The proposal that HIGD1C and COX4I2 are 'key components' (C28) is well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches, though the authors appropriately acknowledge additional components may be required (C106).

results.result: HIGD1C is required for carotid body oxygen sensing and enhances complex IV sensitivity to hypoxia.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 represent the main findings stated in the abstract. These are strongly supported by the comprehensive data from whole-body plethysmography (Figure 2), CSN recordings (Figure 3), calcium imaging (Figure 3), mitochondrial membrane potential measurements (Figure 4), and cell culture oxygen consumption studies (Figure 6). The convergence of evidence from multiple experimental systems at different levels of organization (whole animal, organ, cell, organelle) provides robust support.
